Gluck-Thaler, Aaron. 2023. Surveillance Studies and the History of Artificial Intelligence: A Missed Opportunity? Surveillance & Society 21 (3): 259-268. https://ojs.library.queensu.ca/index.php/surveillance-and-society/index | ISSN: 1477-7487 © The author(s), 2023 | Licensed to the Surveillance Studies Network under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license

Aaron Gluck-Thaler Harvard University, USA aarongluckthaler@g.harvard.edu Abstract

This research note considers how scholars of surveillance might approach the historical legacies that surveillance through artificial intelligence (AI) is implicated in. Engaging with the relative lack of historical studies within the pages of Surveillance & Society, the note argues that in the context of surveillant AI the stakes of an ahistorical analysis are especially high. Bridging scholarship within the history of science with surveillance studies, the note explores how AI techniques today reanimate a longer history of how scientific knowledge production on classification has been coextensive with the maintenance and production of racial, gender, and social hierarchies. The note briefly examines one genealogy––the history of the field of pattern recognition, its relationship to state surveillance, and its understanding of identification as a problem of classification––to consider how surveillance and AI contingently converged. The note concludes by showing how such histories can help scholars of surveillance critically reassess common understandings of the consequences of AI and AI-adjacent surveillance practices used today.

## Introduction

In the inaugural article of Surveillance & Society in 2002, David Lyon argued for the need for historical analysis. Noting gaps in theoretical and empirical understandings of networked surveillance practices, Lyon (2002: 2–3) emphasized that a “key method for situating surveillance situations is to ask historical and comparative questions. If this is how things are done today, was it always like this, and what brought about the changes?” (see also Marx 2002). As I understand it, this was a call for the field of surveillance studies to remain grounded in the historicity of surveillance while being attentive to changes worthy of scrutiny. One implication was that ahistoricism would risk grafting outdated understandings of surveillance onto newer practices. Another implication was that presentism could neglect the various sources from which supposedly new surveillance practices emerged, thereby naturalizing the inevitability of those practices rather than studying their historical contingency.

In the decade that followed this methodological call to action, historical examinations of surveillance were marginal to the field of surveillance studies (see Lauer 2012: 568–570). Since 2011, there are encouraging signs that this has changed. Although relatively few articles within the pages of Surveillance & Society have been historical in focus,1 the field is demonstrably receptive to historical perspectives. Historians are welcomed at conferences and workshops. Historically oriented monographs are favourably reviewed in

# Research Note

# Surveillance Studies and the History of Artificial Intelligence: A Missed Opportunity?

Surveillance & Society.2 Scholars have used archival sources to reorient the field by foregrounding its disciplinary absences, as in Simone Browne’s (2015) use of the archive of transatlantic slavery to show the “absented presence” of blackness in studies of surveillance or Rachel Dubrofsky and Shoshana Magnet’s (2015) critical feminist reading of the foundations of surveillance. Other scholars have recently shown how history can bring contextual specificity to surveillance studies while also enriching the identification of broader trends (see Heynen and Van der Meulen 2019: 3–30; Browne 2019: 306–308; Marklund and Skouvig 2021: 1–19; Lauer and Lipartito 2022: 1–26; Igo 2022: 203–209).

There are still challenges to a more substantial integration of historical methods, scholarship, and forms of explanation within surveillance studies. Scholars of surveillance often pursue theoretical analytics, like panopticism, that helpfully reveal underlying logics shared by a plurality of surveillant scenarios (see also Otter 2008: 1–61). At least within the history of science, many scholars now approach such claims of generalizable regularities with caution (see Daston 2016). One lingering genre of surveillance history similarly poses challenges for a more robust interdisciplinary exchange. Epochal narratives of modernity, the nation state, and bureaucratization can grate against forms of explanation more focused on historical continuities (compare Zuboff 2019 with Lauer and Lipartito 2022; Crain 2021), local contexts (compare Giddens 1981: 157–181, 1985: 41–53 with Heynen and Van der Meulen 2019), or mundane, imperfect, and contested practices of knowledge production (compare Dandeker 1994 with Robertson 2010; Magnet 2011; Gates 2011).

My focus here is not on how to comprehensively address these challenges. Rather, I want to explore the stakes of not addressing them. What is foreclosed by assuming either the novelty or historical universality of surveillance practices used today? What is revealed by attending to the historical contexts that those practices are the products of?

The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and surveillance is an apt context to examine these two questions. Within this area, the stakes of an ahistorical analysis are especially high. Discourses of the novelty of AI have fueled its hype–driven economy and have encouraged its most controversial surveillance applications, like inferring race, gender, and sexual orientation (see Elish and boyd 2018; Broussard 2019; Campolo and Crawford 2020; Kaltheuner 2021; Keyes, Hitzig, and Blell 2021; Buolamwini and Gebru 2018; Keyes 2018). As Ruha Benjamin (2019) has argued, such discourses of novelty and professed advancement erase how racial hierarchies have become encoded in and amplified by algorithmic technologies. Claims of an unprecedented and unstopped “AI revolution”––echoed by national security advisors, corporate executives, computer scientists, and military officials alike (Kissinger, Schmidt, and Huttenlocher 2021; Schmidt et al. 2021)––have further made government desires for surveillance through AI seem like a new phenomenon. To avoid uncritically channeling this discourse of novelty, careful attention to the historical legacies that surveillance through AI is implicated in remains needed.

There are many contexts for such a history. Building on earlier work, recent scholarship within the history of science has maintained a critical distance from accounts of AI written by its practitioners. In place of celebratory narratives of discovery, this scholarship has explored how the advent of AI is inseparable not just from the history of computing but also from overlapping histories of colonialism, state formation, labour, capitalism, disability, gender, and race, across multiple geographies (see, e.g., Dillon et al. 2021; Roberge and Castelle 2021; Penn 2021; Abbate and Dick 2022; Nagy 2022; see also Edwards 1997; Turner 2006). This scholarship is lending complexity to earlier accounts of the “invention” of AI by studying the surprising sites of its emergence, the power relationships involved in its development, and the work that has been required to sustain AI both as a material technology and as a discursive concept (see Cave, Dihal, and Dillon 2020). Under a historical lens, AI techniques for inferring race resuscitate the history of scientific racism, criminal anthropometry, and other classificatory systems for producing hierarchies of human

## The Call

Bridging concerns from history of science scholarship with those of surveillance studies, in what follows, I outline one necessarily brief analysis of the intertwined history of surveillance and AI. My point of entry into this history is perhaps an unexpected object of analysis but I think a suggestive one. In the spirit of unpacking “academic complicity in fueling deterministic narratives of technological change,” I focus on the call by Surveillance & Society for papers for this special section (Surveillance & Society 2022). I do so to suggest the limitations of the field of surveillance studies to address the question of what, if not technology, made the historical convergence between AI and surveillance possible.

Motivated by the present popularity of AI, machine learning, and algorithmic decision-making systems, the call for papers positions two areas as promising sites for inquiry. The first is how “the circulation of terms like AI does powerful cultural work that may reify dangerously limited visions of technological futures.” The second is how AI “may be codifying discriminatory practices in opaque code.” To those ends, the call appropriately suggests studies that respond to the real and lived consequences of AI today. The type of analysis called for is oriented towards the present and future consequences of surveillance through AI. The call is not oriented, to paraphrase Lyon (2002), towards how this came to be: for example, the social, economic, political, or technoscientific historical practices that led to AI and AI-adjacent techniques disproportionately reproducing discriminatory outcomes for historically marginalized groups. The closest acknowledgement of the historicity of surveillance through AI is an inclusion in the list of suggested (but not exhaustive) topics: the “overlaying of AI capabilities with older-generation devices, such as CCTV cameras” (Surveillance & Society 2022).

Omissions like this might be an unavoidable consequence of any transdisciplinary field of inquiry. But they are also cause for scrutiny. So too are the analytical concepts that scholars use to understand surveillance. The call for papers provides a definition to give coherence to the topic of this special section: “To the extent that AI systems have learning capacities, they can be thought of as being surveillant: amassing data, processing it to discover patterns, and acting upon those patterns to shape behavior or actions” (Surveillance & Society 2022). Within this definition, we find a reliance on one keyword: pattern. Indeed, “pattern” is often used to make sense of surveillance through data (see, e.g., Andrejevic and Gates 2014). But pattern, when approached as a historically variable object of scientific knowledge, does not sit outside of the histories of surveillance and AI. A partial history of pattern helps to clarify what, at least in part, made the convergence between surveillance and AI possible.

## Towards Histories of Surveillance & Artificial Intelligence

One genealogy of AI-enabled techniques today is how their historical emergence was tied to an epistemic shift in the nature of patterns. In the mid-1950s in the United States, new definitions of pattern coalesced within the technical field of pattern recognition. These notions broke from earlier understandings of patterns by scientists, like patterns that could be recognized in culture by anthropologists or those that, psychologists reasoned, were holistically perceived by humans. Often in conversation with those fields (Halpern 2015: 145–212; Lee 2020: 87–127; Chun 2021: 205–213; Geoghegan 2022: 53–84) and in the legacy of older scientific practices of pattern seeking (Daston and Galison 2007: 309–361; Waycott 2019), the field of pattern recognition transformed patterns into a technical object of scientific knowledge. Formal descriptions could define patterns, mathematical techniques could classify them, and machines could recognize them. For example, in an early paper on pattern recognition, researcher Oliver Selfridge (1956: 164)  argued that “a pattern is recognizable. This is an operational definition.” This was not a statement of metaphysics––that patterns exist in the world as entities independent from human interpretation. This was a statement of utility:

that “a pattern is determined by the rules for recognizing it rather than vice versa” (Selfridge 1956: 164). Bypassing questions of which patterns already existed in the world, pattern recognition researchers brought their own patterns into being. Squares would not be recognized using a priori notions of idealized squares. Rather, computers would find the features of squares that best classified photographs of squares against photographs of other shapes (Selfridge 1955; Dinneen 1955).

This statistical, mechanized, and nominalist answer to the problem of what was relevant to the identity of visual objects was historically consequential. As Aaron Mendon-Plasek (2021) has argued, the field of pattern recognition helped to inaugurate a problem framing strategy that valorized reliable performance and sensitivity to context while classifying complex sets of data. Mostly distinct from early work in AI, this practice first came into the field of machine learning and only later into artificial intelligence, particularly in the 1980s, as practitioners turned to machine learning (Mendon-Plasek 2021, also on the role of optical character recognition in pattern recognition research; see also Plasek 2016). Work in pattern recognition similarly prefigured the instrumentalist approach to prediction in the data sciences (Jones 2018; see also Mackenzie 2016). As Wendy Chun (2021) has recently argued, this process of recognition through patterns was tied up in a historical shift to the politics of recognition, something still central to algorithmic practices of identification today (see Apprich et al. 2018).

The field of artificial intelligence had a complex and changing relationship to work in pattern recognition. In the 1950s, the formal, mathematical, and instrumental approach to pattern provided artificial intelligence practitioners with fodder both for mythologizing the origins of their research and for funding that research (see Simon 1997: 8–10; McCorduck 2004: 156–160; Boden 2008: 321–323; Newell and Simon 1957; cf. Newell 1982; see also Dick 2015). Pattern recognition researchers were similarly responsive to developments in AI, especially when controversies suggested changing patronage relationships (see Olazaran 1993, 1996). The boundary between what distinguished a pattern recognition researcher from an artificial intelligence researcher was also often in flux. Groups researching AI like the Stanford Research Institute (SRI)’s Artificial Intelligence Center first found their footing in pattern recognition research (Nilsson 2009: 89–111, 1965). Particularly while working on problems of visual recognition, practitioners were wont to frame their work as contributing to a shared project (see, e.g., Selfridge and Neisser 1960; Rosen 1967; Nilsson 1968; Gose 1969; Kanal and Chandrasekaran 1969: 317–319; Gelsema and Kanal 1988: 483).

Still, from the 1950s through the 1970s much research in pattern recognition was carried out separately from work in AI. Significantly, the field of pattern recognition produced and kept alive a core practice of identification that was often peripheral to work in AI (see, e.g., Chandrasekaran and Goel 1988). This practice was informed by a central epistemic assumption: that the identity of individual objects could be recognized by mathematical classification techniques operating on datasets populated with other objects. Recognition of individual identity was taken as equivalent to the classification of an object in a given population, as computed by measures of extent of group membership. As Marvin Minsky put it at the 1959 Eastern Joint Computer Conference: “the things we call patterns are classes of signals or figures, not single figures. They are classes of figures which are grouped together because, for some purpose or other, they can be treated alike” (Bledsoe et al. 1959: 234).

This approach to identification supported the expansion of the field of pattern recognition, despite critiques that the recognition of identity was not reducible to its classification (Sayre 1965; see also Dreyfus 1965: 39–42). As two practitioners characterized the field: “whatever successes we have had in the field have been a result of an effective transformation of a perception-recognition problem into just such a classification problem” (Kanal and Chandrasekaran 1969: 321). With this approach, by 1968, pattern recognition practitioners could argue that patterns were both everywhere and primed for classification. Patterns were not just in text and speech but also in “fingerprints, electrocardiograms, radar echoes from celestial bodies, engine noises, seismic events, white blood cells, clouds, diseases, nuclear events (in bubble chamber photographs or spark chamber tracks), leaves, insects, psychopathies, faces, and so on” (Eden 1968: 210; on speech recognition research, see Li and Mills 2019; on bubble chamber pattern recognition research, see

Galison 1997: 384–411). With their instruments––often some combination of photocell mosaics, scanners, digital computers, memory modules, algorithms, and mathematical classification techniques––pattern recognition researchers began transforming the world into classifiable patterns.

In practice, pattern recognition researchers tended to focus on patterns that were relevant to the security priorities of the US government agencies that funded them, like tanks in aerial photographs (see, e.g., Harley et al. 1963; Nilsson 2009: 105–109). Many “new” technologies using AI techniques today, like facial recognition, emerged from patronage relationships between pattern recognition researchers and government agencies (on government patronage of AI, see Edwards 1997: 239–273; see also Whittaker 2021: 50–55; Crawford 2021: 151–209). Consider the pattern recognition work of Woodrow “Woody” Wilson Bledsoe, which began in the late 1950s in research on optical character recognition. Like his pattern recognition colleagues, Bledsoe (1960: 1) also held that “the problem of pattern recognition is one of dividing a collection of things into classes.” Under sponsorship by cover companies of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) through the 1960s, Bledsoe developed an early facial recognition technique (Raviv 2020; see also Gates 2011: 28–32; Lee-Morrison 2019: 57–84; Stevens and Keyes 2021: 3–6). Bledsoe founded a company called Panoramic Research, Incorporated (PRI) to conduct this research, which he later mythologized as “one of the first AI groups before the term ‘Artificial Intelligence’ came into use” (qtd. in Ballantyne, Boyer, and Hines 1996: 9). At PRI, Bledsoe and his colleagues researched applications of their pattern recognition techniques, like face identification within a population of over a million people (Bledsoe 1964a: 1–6, 1964b: 2).

Although work in pattern recognition like Bledsoe’s was shaped by state surveillance priorities, pattern recognition researchers also helped to produce those priorities. Researchers like Oliver Selfridge sat on highranking scientific advisory committees that reformed US intelligence agencies in the 1950s and 1960s. Unsurprisingly, these committees provided advice that was attentive to work in pattern recognition. Recommendations for “Large-scale machine processing of essentially all intercepted material” accompanied calls for word recognition machines and mechanized Morse code processing techniques (Special Intelligence Panel of the Science Advisory Committee to the President 1958: 29–51). Concurrently at MIT’s Lincoln Laboratory, Selfridge supervised the development of these very same techniques (Eisenstadt et al. 1957). Government desires for new surveillance capabilities did not determine scientific work in pattern recognition but were co-extensive with it. Caught in the Cold War interplay of flush government support, international conflict, and expansive technoscientific ambition, surveillance and science made each other.

## AI & Surveillance Today

Turning to histories like this helps to decenter the supposed novelty of surveillance through AI techniques today. The history of pattern recognition shows how many of the “biases” of AI-driven surveillance systems are rooted in longer histories of classification (for a sampling of such histories, see, e.g., Bowker and Star 2000: 195–225; Cole 2001: 32–118; Nakamura 2002: 101–135; Wernimont 2018: 17–85; Noble 2018: 134– 152; Crawford 2021: 151–179; see also Lyon 2005; Benjamin 2019). For example, in reports to CIA front companies Bledsoe (1964b: 24–25) cited Alphonse Bertillon’s criminal anthropometry and Cesare Lombroso’s phrenological work on the “criminal man.” Using photographs that were probably only of white men, Bledsoe (1966: 1–27) updated these standards for the digital computer, creating “standard heads” to better locate facial features. To the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) and to CIA front companies, Bledsoe (1963, 1965) pitched still persistent extensions of this work, like “using facial characteristics as a means for identifying a person’s racial background and/or maturation environment” (Bledsoe 1965: 1) or having a machine “first decide whether the person is male or female, then decide whether the person is Oriental or not, etc.” (Bledsoe 1963: 3).

When framed historically, the biases of facial recognition technologies are not merely the products of illconsidered decisions by computer programmers. Rather, as numerous scholars have similarly argued (see Gates 2011: 1–24; Magnet 2011: 19–50; Browne 2015: 90–129; Benjamin 2019: 67–87; Crawford 2021: 123–149; Chun 2021: 185–229; Stark and Hutson 2021: 922–978), the discriminatory outcomes of facial

recognition reanimate a longer genealogy of how scientific knowledge production on classification has–– willfully or not––been co-extensive with the maintenance and production of racial, gender, and social hierarchies. Such histories also push against narratives of technological determinism: that the “invention” of AI caused new surveillance capabilities. Before surveillant AI systems were built, scientists put new concepts like an instrumentalized understanding of pattern to work in making the fit between surveillance and automated classification techniques possible, desirable, and actualized. The historical discontinuities of pattern recognition research are equally significant. Here, as elsewhere, practices characteristic to the Cold War activated already existing forms of scientific knowledge, like patterns, and stamped them with a distinctive form: instrumentalized, state-funded, concerned with matters of security, and often propelled by scientific hubris (see generally Mody 2008; Heyck and Kaiser 2010; Wilson and Kaiser 2014; Oreskes 2021).

The pervasiveness of surveillant AI in areas as varied as employment screening and border control does strike me as a noteworthy shift from more restricted historical deployments of such technologies (see Ajunwa 2020; Molnar 2019). But there is more at stake to AI-driven technologies today than their ubiquitous use and consequences. Such technologies are only possible in specific historical contexts, many of which are still in need of critical examination. I have briefly explored two interconnected contexts: one in which the visual world was transformed into data-based patterns primed for classification and one in which the technical field dedicated to doing so became closely aligned with state surveillance priorities.

Some of the most exciting recent studies of surveillance have carefully attended to the multiple historical genealogies of surveillance (see Browne 2015; Lauer 2017; Igo 2018; Hochman 2022). This work has avoided neatly packaged theoretical analytics and epochal historical narratives to instead focus on the ambiguous meanings, deeply rooted hierarchies, and knowledge practices that have sustained surveillance. Studies limited to contemporary surveillance practices, whether from sociology, political science, or geography, are no less important. I have emphasized, however, a continued and increasingly urgent need to complement such studies with historical examinations of the practices that have made seemingly new surveillance techniques possible.
